_comment: safety batch D English body (2026-11-06). Inspect by the UK AI Security Institute and Meridian Labs. Facts only from the official docs front page, repository README and LICENSE captured on 2026-11-06; anything else is recorded as unknown.

axes.model_access: The official docs front page states "Built-in support for over 20 model providers" and names local inference with HuggingFace, vLLM and SGLang. The quick-start tabs pair `pip install openai` + `export OPENAI_API_KEY`, then Anthropic, Google and `hf/...` + `HF_TOKEN`, each run with `--model openai/...` style selectors. The full provider list and per-provider capability differences were not inventoried.
axes.runtime: `pip install inspect-ai` into your own Python environment; the main entry point is the terminal command `inspect eval` (docs example: `inspect eval simpleqa.py --model ...`). The same page lists the web-based Inspect View tool for monitoring and visualizing evaluations and a VS Code extension for authoring and debugging. Execution happens on your machine inside the sandbox you choose; an official hosted cloud line: not stated officially.
axes.local_files: An evaluation is a Task written in `.py` (Dataset + Solver + Scorer), and datasets can be loaded straight from HuggingFace with `hf_dataset()`. The docs front page lists "over 200 pre-built evaluations ready to run on any model", and its table of contents has Log Files, Inspect View and Task Views entries. The default log directory name and file layout were not verified verbatim in this pass.
axes.background: Local batch execution: the docs table of contents lists Running Eval Sets, Parallelism, Handling Errors, Setting Limits, Checkpointing and Intervention, i.e. parallel eval sets, checkpoints and human intervention are documented concepts. Whether a task continues elsewhere after your machine shuts down: not stated officially - Inspect is not a hosted service.
axes.tools: The docs front page lists built-in bash, python, text editing, web search and computer tools, and states support for custom and MCP tools; the table of contents adds Tool Approval, Tool Result Review, Agent Bridge and Extensions. The same page describes running arbitrary external agents as the subject under test, naming Claude Code, Codex CLI and Gemini CLI.
axes.context: The table of contents lists Compaction, Caching, Fallbacks, Multimodal and Structured Output on the model side, plus Multiple Scorers, Scoring Policy and Model Grading on the scoring side. Cross-session memory is not its model: one evaluation run, one log. Default compaction strategy and thresholds: no official text captured in this pass.
axes.permissions: MIT (LICENSE text read directly; copyright holder is the UK AI Security Institute). It runs in your environment and model calls go through the providers and keys you configure. The docs front page describes a sandboxing system for "running untrusted model code" in Docker, Kubernetes, Modal, Proxmox, Vagrant and other systems via an extension API, and the table of contents adds Sandboxing, Approvers, Hooks and Filesystems. Telemetry and data-upload terms: no official statement captured in this pass.
axes.fit: Fits: writing your own evals and agent tasks, putting untrusted model code into a sandbox, keeping tool approval plus local logs for sample-by-sample review, and running one task definition across 20+ providers. Not a fit: wanting only a hosted console, needing a metric library without maintaining Python evaluations, or treating somebody else's leaderboard numbers as the deliverable.

sections.变更记录说明: No changelog text was read in this pass: the docs front page navigation exposes a CHANGELOG entry (listed in the sources), which was not reviewed item by item. Cadence comes from repository metadata: the last push is dated 2026-11-06 (GitHub API verified the same day) and the repository is not flagged as archived, so `lifecycle` is recorded as active; the concrete contents of each release were not inventoried and remain unverified.
sections.第一次怎么用:
1. Decide the model access first: the official quick-start pattern is "install the matching SDK + export the API key", and local inference goes through HuggingFace / vLLM / SGLang.
2. `pip install inspect-ai`, then run the first task with `inspect eval <task.py> --model <provider/model>`.
3. If the model executes code or touches files, read the official Sandboxing position first and put the task into a sandbox backend such as Docker, then consider tool approval.
4. To go through results sample by sample use the Inspect View tool listed in the docs; for authoring and debugging the official docs recommend (but do not require) the VS Code extension.
5. For batch runs, use the docs entries on Eval Sets and Parallelism rather than writing your own loop.

runs:
**This site has not completed end-to-end measured runs.** `inspect eval` was not executed, Inspect View logs were not opened, and this entry produces no scores, accuracies or rankings, nor any audit of the pre-built evaluation list.

This section only organizes statements from the official docs front page and the repository README (installation, model providers and local inference, sandbox backends, tools and MCP, tool approval, logs and viewers, external agent runs), each tied to the sources list and the verification date. The docs Tutorial and Options pages were not captured on the day.

**Suggested measurements** (all pointing at things the official readable pages do not answer):

- Cost and friction of running one task against a second provider, including fallback behaviour
- The practical boundary between Tool Approval and a Docker sandbox when the model emits shell commands
- Whether checkpoint/intervention resume works across two separate host runs
